vignette:
He is 73 now, a divorced North American man who has spent most of his life as a journalist, and when he talks about the event, he still tells it the way he learned to tell stories for a living: in sequence, with dates, places, and the kind of detail that makes an audience lean in. But when he gets closer to the disaster itself, his voice changes. The facts remain intact, yet the feeling in the room shifts. He goes still, then brisk, as if speed can protect him from what he remembers.

Decades earlier, he is working as a reporter in a city that prides itself on being orderly until the day a man-made catastrophe tears through it. He is sent to cover the scene, initially thinking of it as another assignment with deadlines and telephone calls and the ordinary friction of getting quotes before deadline. He arrives expecting smoke, noise, confusion. Instead, he is met with a level of destruction that feels designed rather than accidental, a kind of violence that leaves him with the sick sense that human hands made this. People are running, shouting, searching. Sirens overlap and vanish. He remembers the smell first-burnt material, dust, something metallic-and then the faces. He sees a child with one shoe, a woman repeating a name, a man staring at his own hands as if they belong to someone else. He is there to observe, but his body behaves as though it is trapped inside the event. His heart pounds, his mouth goes dry, and he cannot decide where to put his eyes.

In the weeks that follow, he keeps working. Journalism becomes both shield and obligation. He files stories, attends briefings, and interviews survivors with a steadiness that others mistake for composure. At home, however, the event does not stay in the newsroom. He starts waking before dawn with a jolt, already tense, already listening for something he cannot identify. He notices himself checking exits in restaurants and public buildings, sitting with his back to walls, scanning faces on the street. He tells himself these are habits of a good reporter, someone trained to notice everything. Yet the vigilance feels different now-less professional than desperate, as if danger is always arriving a second before he does.

He tries to keep the memories in order, but they come in fragments. A sound from a television sends him back to the scene. The smell of smoke from a neighbor's grill can drop him into a cold, hollow state in which he is no longer in his kitchen but standing amid wreckage, helpless and angry. He begins avoiding anniversary coverage, memorials, and certain neighborhoods. He changes the channel when footage appears. He leaves family gatherings early if conversation turns to disasters, politics, or public safety. At times he is aware that he is slipping away from the lives around him, yet he cannot stop himself. Even now, as an older man, he describes a familiar sensation of being elsewhere while his body remains seated in the present.

His marriage does not survive the years that follow. He does not blame everything on the trauma, but he knows it altered the shape of his life at home. He becomes irritable, distant, and preoccupied. His then-wife complains that he is listening for things no one else can hear. She is right. At night he checks windows and locks more than once. He startles easily at sudden noises. There are periods when he feels an intense, unshakable anger-not only at those responsible for the disaster, but at the world for allowing such cruelty to exist. Other times the feeling is closer to shame, a private conviction that he should have done more, seen more, prevented more, even though he knows rationally that he was a reporter, not a rescuer.

In session, he speaks with pride about the career he built, the articles he wrote, the years he spent chasing truth. Yet he also speaks of a narrowing that happened around the trauma. He no longer walks into crowded events without calculating exits. He no longer watches the news without bracing. Sleep remains broken; dreams place him back amid chaos, where he is always too late, always trying to reach someone just out of range. He rises in the morning with a body that feels older than its years, already tired from the effort of staying alert.

Still, he continues to work, even into later life, because reporting gives structure to days that otherwise feel vulnerable and unmoored. He moves through the world with care, measuring sounds, planning routes, keeping his distance from scenes that resemble the one that changed him. What remains most vivid to him is not only the destruction but the helplessness of witnessing it, and how that helplessness has followed him quietly through the decades, shaping the way he sleeps, the way he listens, the way he enters every room.
